﴿When he envies﴾: when his envy becomes apparent and he acts upon its requirement, by seeking to harm the envied person. It is reported from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz: "I have not seen a wrongdoer more like the wronged than the envier." It is also permissible that the evil of the envier refers to his sin, the ugliness of his condition at the time of his envy, and his showing its effect.

It also includes what those who are not responsible do by eating, biting, stinging and gnawing, like beasts of prey and insects, and what God has placed in inanimate things of various kinds of harm, such as burning in fire and killing by poison.

*Al-Ghasiq* is the night when its darkness becomes thick, from His saying: ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. From it comes *ghasaqat al-'ayn*, meaning the eye became filled with tears, and *ghasaqat al-jurah*, meaning the wound became filled with blood. *Waqabuhu* means the entry of its darkness into everything. It is said: *waqabat al-shams*, when the sun set.

In a hadith: when he saw the sun had set, he said, "This is the time for its prohibition," meaning the Maghrib prayer. [[Abu 'Ubayd related it in *Gharib al-Hadith* through the chain of 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Uqbah as a mursal report.]]

It is also said that *al-Ghasiq* is the moon when it is full. From 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took my hand, pointed to the moon and said, "Seek refuge in God from the evil of this, for it is *al-ghasiq* when it sets." [[Al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Ya'la all related it through Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Khalid, al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Salamah, from her.]] *Waqabuhu* means its entry into the eclipse and its blackening. It is also permissible that *al-Ghasiq* refers to the black snake, and *waqabahu* means he struck it and pierced it.

*Al-Waqb* means piercing. From it comes *waqbat al-tharid*, meaning the hollow of the broth bowl. The seeking of refuge from the evil of the night is because its spreading is greater in it, and guarding against it is more difficult. From it comes their saying: "The night is more hidden for calamity," and their saying: "The night has become treacherous," because when it grows dark, betrayal increases in it. The evil is attributed to it because it is connected to it, as its occurrence happens in it.

﴿From the evil of the blowers in knots﴾: the women, or the souls, or the groups of sorceresses who tie knots in threads and blow over them and recite incantations. [[He (al-Zamakhshari) said: "They are the sorceresses who tie the threads and blow over them..." Ibn al-Munayyir (Ahmad) said: It has already been mentioned that the principle of the Qadariyyah (a Mu'tazilite-associated school that denied divine decree over human acts) is to deny the reality of sorcery, though the Book and the Sunnah have established that it occurs and have commanded seeking refuge from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) was himself bewitched with a comb and combings in a male palm-spathe, and the hadith is well known. Al-Zamakhshari was provoked by his passions until he denied what is known, and he only follows his Mu'tazilite creed and covers the face of the sun with his palm.]] *Al-nafth* is blowing with saliva, and there is no effect in that. [[His saying "and there is no effect in that" is based on the Mu'tazilite doctrine that sorcery has no reality and no effect. The People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) affirmed it and affirmed its effect, on the apparent evidence of the Book and the Sunnah. (Ed.)]] Except if there is a feeding of something harmful, or giving it to drink, or making him smell it, or direct contact with the thing used for bewitchment in some manner. But God, mighty and majestic, may act at that time as a trial that distinguishes the steadfast upon the truth from the ignorant masses of the common people. The Hashwiyyah (literalists) and the rabble (*al-ra'a'*) attribute it to them and their blowing, while those firm in the firm word do not turn to that nor pay it any heed. [[His saying "the Hashwiyyah and the rabble attribute it" — in the *Sihah*, *al-ra'a'* means the young and base people; and there, *al-tagham* means the lowest of people, and *al-wagh* means the lowly man who serves for the sake of his stomach. (Ed.)]]

If you ask: What is the meaning of seeking refuge from their evil? I answer: There are three aspects. The first is that one seeks refuge from their practice, which is the craft of sorcery, and from their sin in it. The second is that one seeks refuge from their tempting people by their sorcery and from the falsehood by which they deceive them. The third is that one seeks refuge from the evil God may cause at their blowing. It is also permissible that they refer to the cunning women, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾ (12:28), comparing their guile to sorcery and to blowing on the knot.

Or those who tempt men by exposing themselves to them and displaying their beauty, as if they bewitch them thereby.

﴿When he envies﴾: when his envy becomes apparent and he acts upon its requirement, by seeking to harm the envied person. For if the effect of what he conceals does not appear, no harm returns from it upon the one he envies. Rather, it harms himself, through his distress at another's happiness. It is reported from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz: "I have not seen a wrongdoer more like the wronged than the envier." It is also permissible that the evil of the envier refers to his sin, the ugliness of his condition at the time of his envy, and his showing its effect.

If you ask: His saying "from the evil of what He has created" is a generalization over everything one seeks refuge from; so what is the meaning of seeking refuge after it from the night, the blowers and the envier? I answer: The evil of these was singled out from every evil because its matter is hidden, and because it reaches a person from where he does not know, as if he were assassinated by it. They said: "The worst enemy is the treacherous one who plots against you when you do not perceive it."

If you ask: Why was some of what one seeks refuge from defined and some indefinite? I answer: "The blowers" was made definite because every blower is evil. "Ghasiq" was made indefinite because not every dark night contains evil; evil is in some and not others. Likewise, not every envier does harm. And there is a praiseworthy envy, which is envy in good things. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no envy except in two." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them; al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.]]

Abu Tammam said:

"And I am envied, and I excuse my envious ones...
and my envier in noble deeds is no envier."
[[Abu Tammam's lines. He means: I combine praiseworthy qualities, so envy is a metaphor for that. "Excuse" (*'adhara*) is like *daraba yadribu*, meaning my envier is excused because of the goodness and greatness of my qualities; and the envier in praiseworthy qualities is not a blameworthy envier, but one who is envied in praise.]]

And he said:

"Boast, for no heaven of nobility has risen
except that your good deeds are its pillars.
Excuse your envier for what you have been singled out with,
for nobility is fine when envy is in its like."
[[Also Abu Tammam's lines. He likened the elevated quality to heaven, and used it as a metaphor in the explicit manner; elevation is a supporting metaphor, since it is proper to perceptible things. He likened beautiful deeds to the pillars of heaven with an eloquent comparison, because through them comes moral elevation.]]

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the two protective surahs (*al-mu'awwidhatayn*) is as if he had recited all the Books God has sent down." [[Al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi related it with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. It has been mentioned more than once that these are weak, and that the hadith traced to the Prophet on this is fabricated; God knows best.]]

Meccan, though it is said to be Medinan, and its verses number 5. "It was revealed after the Elephant." In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*Al-Falaq* and *al-Farq* both mean the dawn, because the night is split open and separated from it. It is a form in the sense of the passive participle (*maf'ul*). It is said in a proverb: "He is clearer than the splitting of dawn, and than the separation of dawn." From this comes their saying: "*al-Furqan* has shone," meaning the dawn has risen.

It is also said that *al-Falaq* is everything God splits open: the earth for plants, the mountains for springs, the clouds for rain, the wombs for offspring, grains and date-stones, and other things. It is also said that it is a valley in Hell, named from the expression for a low, level piece of ground (*ma iṭma'anna min al-ard*), and that the plural is *falaqan*. It is reported from one of the Companions that he came to Syria and saw the houses of the People of the Covenant (*ahl al-dhimmah*) and the ease of living they enjoyed and the worldly comfort granted to them. He said, "I am not concerned. Is there not behind them *al-Falaq*?" It was asked, "And what is *al-Falaq*?" He said, "A house in Hell which, when opened, all the people of the Fire cry out because of the intensity of its heat."
